5099.dq: En Kongo, les mots ont, dans la règle, l'accent principal (étymologique) sur la syllabe radicale et un accent secondaire (rythmique) assez fort sur la pénultième.

5099.prule: Main (etymological) accent on the root syllable, i.e. the first syllable of the stem after the class prefix; class prefixes as a rule do not bear or shift it (Laman & Heinitz 1922 §2a: 'The root-accent always falls on the root-syllable... Prefixes, as a rule, have no influence on the accent'). The language is tonal, and tone-driven 'melodic intensity' may weaken but never remove the root accent.
5099.srule: One fairly strong secondary (rhythmic) accent on the penultimate syllable (Laman 1936 §20: 'un accent secondaire (rythmique) assez fort sur la pénultième'); the same author's 1922 study adds that it is weakened when the ultima takes strong stress (Laman & Heinitz 1922 §2b, p. 1).
5099.quote: Cette intensité mélodique ne doit pas être confondue avec ce qu'on appelle en général l'accent d'intensité ou même, tout simplement, l'accent. 20. En Kongo, les mots ont, dans la règle, l'accent principal (étymologique) sur la syllabe radicale et un accent secondaire (rythmique) assez fort sur la pénultième. L'intensité mélodique peut affaiblir plus ou moins l'accent étymologique sur la syllabe radicale, mais celle-ci ne peut jamais devenir atone.

5099.tone: Kongo is tonal. Laman 1936 §22: the monosyllabic radicals show 'quatre tons très caractéristiques' (bas/grave, haut fort accentué, haut, moyen), 'Ces quatre tons des radicaux servent à former les quatre principales classes tonales, qui sont l’origine des tons sémantiques et des tons grammaticaux. Ils constituent aussi le principe de la notation mélodique dans le dictionnaire'. §19 ties tone to intensity and length (high, long, rising/falling syllables are more intense; 'L’ultième au ton plus haut que la syllabe précédente a toujours une très grande intensité') and separates this 'intensité mélodique' from 'l’accent d’intensité ou même, tout simplement, l’accent'; §20 says tone may weaken but never remove the root accent. Laman & Heinitz 1922 §28: 'The strong stress in the Kongo language may be placed on different syllables, whether they are high or low, rising or falling, because pitch and position in the sentence may have a strong influence upon the accent' (scan 'maj', 'risini', '£' normalised). De Clercq 1907 p. 451 marks long vowels with a macron and 'l’accent tonique par ’' and says speakers draw out long vowels 'en haussant légèrement la voix d’une façon presque chantante', but states no tone system and no placement rule.

a̋: ton haut fort accentué, aigu double (classe aiguë double, mélodie descendante)

tn.quote: nous trouvons quatre tons très caractéristiques: le ton bas à, grave, le ton haut fort accentué a̋, aigu double, le ton haut á, aigu, le ton moyen ā, aigu moyen. ... Ces quatre tons des radicaux servent à former les quatre principales classes tonales, qui sont l'origine des tons sémantiques et des tons grammaticaux. ... à indiquant la classe grave de mélodie montante; a̋ indiquant la classe aiguë double de mélodie descendante; á indiquant la classe aiguë de mélodie descendante; ā indiquant la classe (aiguë) moyen de mélodie uniforme.
tn.translation: we find four very characteristic tones: the low tone à, grave; the strongly accented high tone a̋, double acute; the high tone á, acute; the mid tone ā, mid acute. ... These four radical tones serve to form the four principal tone classes, which are the origin of the semantic and grammatical tones. ... à marking the grave class with rising melody; a̋ the double-acute class with descending melody; á the acute class with descending melody; ā the mid (acute) class with uniform melody.
tn.cite: Laman, K. E. 1936. Dictionnaire kikongo-français avec une étude phonétique décrivant les dialectes les plus importants de la langue dite kikongo. Mémoires de l'Institut Royal Colonial Belge, Section des sciences morales et politiques, t. II. Bruxelles

tn.note: Four root tones (low à, strongly accented high a̋, high á, mid ā) define four melody classes; rising/falling tones 'play no significant role'; root accent separate (§20); §27 a high lowers a next high

5100.prule: No positional rule is stated for Yoncalla. The source's own object is Mary's River (Central Kalapuya), where phonemic stress, realized with higher pitch ('pitch accent'), falls on the first syllable of the stem and does not move under prefixation; Jacobs's family-general statement (unpublished ms, 'n.p.') puts pitch accent on every syllable felt to be an independent root. Stress is independent of vowel length.

5101.prule: Primary stress always on the first syllable of the word (left-footed, left-headed); quantity-insensitive; no reference to syllable count or weight.

5103.tone: Lord 2016 describes Yora as having lexical tone and grammatical tone (p. 17: 'grammatical tone (in addition to lexical tone)'). High tone is marked with an acute on two-syllable nouns only where grammatical tone is under discussion (p. 16). In §2.3 ergative case on one noun class is marked 'by a certain tone pattern plus nasalization': afa 'his mother' ABS has level (phonetically mid-high) tone and no nasalization, ERG ã́fã has high-low tone plus nasalization; koĩ 'smoke' ABS is high-low plus nasal and takes suffix -nĩ in the ergative (pp. 29-31). Lexical tone on verb roots is also grammatically active (§4.2.3.1, pp. 91-97): the switch-reference allomorphs -yaino/-yaifono, -yaitõ/-yaifafẽ replace -aino/-aifono, -aitõ/-aifafẽ 'if the root to which they are suffixed has two syllables, ends in “a” and the second syllable has low tone, or, if the stem to which it is suffixed has an even number of syllables and ends in “a”' (p. 91). 5104.prule: Lexical pitch accent (mora-based 'ascending kernel' 昇り核 system), not stress: for an n-mora noun there are n+1 contrastive patterns, unaccented (mid pitch, marked !) or the pitch rise on any one of the n moras (kernel /「/ before that mora); the kernel position is a lexical property of the word and is not computable from mora count, syllable count or weight (e.g. 2-mora: !パナ 'nose' unaccented, 「プニ 'boat' initial, パ「ナ 'flower' final; 3-mora: !タタミ, 「ウイビ, ワ「ラビ, アブ「ラ). Restriction: a moraic phoneme (long-vowel second half, N, diphthong offglide) bears the kernel only in absolute word-final position.

5104.tone: The source treats the system entirely as pitch accent (アクセント, 核, ピッチの上昇位置): an 'ascending kernel' marks the mora where pitch rises; n-mora nouns show n+1 patterns including an unaccented type spoken at mid pitch; pitch range is small and 'delayed rise' is common (§3.3). The words 強勢/ストレス/強弱 (stress) do not occur anywhere in the article (a full-text search of the full text: 0 hits); intensity is mentioned only in passing: the initial-kernel type begins slightly higher and 'is pronounced strongly and clearly' while the unaccented type passes if said 'with a little less force, lower' (§3.3), and particle-focused pronunciation makes ヌ 'clearly high and strong' (§3.6, body text). Uwano refutes the earlier N-pattern (2-3 pattern) analyses of Hirayama et al. 1966, Sakimura 1986 and Nakamoto & Shinozaki 1989.

tn.translation: Yoron Higashi-ku dialect is not an N-pattern accent such as the 3-pattern type of earlier studies, but a 'Pn = n+1 multi-pattern accent system' distinguished by an 'ascending kernel'. ... From (8), n-mora words have n+1 distinctions, the types being distinguished from one another by the position of the pitch rise; i.e. a dialect with an ascending kernel /「/, and (8) is interpreted as (9). ... Kernel-less may be left unmarked, but when it must be shown '!' is prefixed, since it is pronounced at roughly 'mid' height. ... 5109.heavy: Closed syllables: 'penultimate closed syllables' (ta-báshti, ta-búyta, ta-búybu) and 'an initial heavy syllable' (púydara, bállata, the latter with a base-generated geminate /l:/); gemination of the following consonant is used 'to make the stress-avoiding syllable heavy' (dójjo 'body', tí-bba 'my husband'); Spanish loans optionally insert a coda (basu ~ bajsu) in the stressed syllable. No vowel-length criterion is stated for weight.
5109.dflt: Left-to-right iambic footing with final-syllable extrametricality: primary on the rightmost foot head = penult in odd-syllable words, antepenult in even-syllable words of four or more, first syllable in disyllables (primary-only grids 2..8: 10 010 0100 00010 000100 0000010 00000100), earlier foot heads secondary; overridden by stress-attracting prefixes (tá-sibë 'our house' vs ti-síbë 'my house') and by diacritically marked roots.
5109.prule: Default: iambic (right-headed) binary feet built from the left edge of the word with the final syllable extrametrical; primary stress on the head of the rightmost foot, so penult in odd-syllable words (pojóre 'canoe', three syllables) and antepenult in even-syllable words of four or more (tipójore 'my canoe', four syllables), a disyllable being stressed on its first syllable (mála); primary stress never leaves a two-syllable right-edge window (ti-memé-shama, tàlipá-newe). Weight override: a closed (heavy) penult takes stress over foot structure and over stress-attracting prefixes (ta-báshti 'our wife'); a heavy initial syllable in an unaffixed trisyllable takes stress (púydara, bállata); a heavy antepenult is otherwise ignored to avoid clash (aròpajtíya); heavy penult beats heavy antepenult (i-shojtó-jti-ø-w). Author hedges: 'Further research is needed to determine the exact role heaviness plays'.
5109.srule: All foot heads are stressed and only the rightmost is primary, so every earlier foot head carries secondary stress: with iambs counted from the left edge and the final syllable extrametrical (unstressable for secondary as for primary stress), secondary stress falls by default on the 2nd (and 4th) syllable from the left (a-jàmisá-jti-ø=ya, achàmatíjsha; 2014 yurùjaré-tu, ti-pòjoré-ni); lexically footed stress-attracting prefixes (ta-, pa-, ma-, ka-, li-, la-, co-operative object prefixes) and closed syllables form feet of their own and keep secondary stress when a later head is primary (tà-pojóre, tà-sibë́=chi, tà-pantálu, 2014 òtto-máshi-tu); adjacent heavy/stress-attracting syllables are not both stressed (clash avoidance). Same footing in compounds (tàlipá-newe).

5110.dq: En yurutí las raíces verbales se componen de una a tres sílabas y no poseen un acento fijo, sino que éste varía bajo influencia de los morfemas que se le sufijan. (p.48) — cf. p.37: 'cuando hay una relajación en el patrón de acentuación en la palabra donde se encuentra'; Barnes 1999 p.212: 'one accented syllable per phonological word'.
5110.dloc: sec. 7.1 'Fonética y Fonología', p.31; sec. 7.3 'Resumen', pp.39-40; sec. 8.1.2 'El Verbo', p.48.
5110.prule: No positional stress rule is stated. The only first-hand open source reports isolated lexical pitch contrasts (author unsure whether tonal or accentual: guacamaya [mã:˥] 'macaw' vs camino [mã:˧] 'path'), says accentual patterns were identified but not characterised, and states that verb roots have no fixed accent: the accent moves under the influence of the suffixes attached. Family surveys code Yurutí as a two-level pitch/tone system (Ardila 1998: two phonological pitch levels, YR dii 'sangre' vs díí 'carne'; Barnes 1999, from Kinch & Kinch ms: pitch accent, one accented (high-pitched) syllable per phonological word). Coded as a tone/pitch-accent system with no stress rule.
5110.srule: None stated. Barnes 1999 (family survey, Yurutí data second-hand from Kinch & Kinch ms): 'Some of the languages, such as Desano, Tuyuca, Yuruti and Cubeo, have one accented syllable per phonological word' (no secondary or alternating accent, unlike Secoya). Not mentioned in Valencia Pérez 2014 (ch. 7 'Fonología' pp.31-40 and sec. 8.1.2 p.48 read).

5111.dq: Generalizing across Mixtec varieties, Josserand (1983:180) defines the couplet as “composed of two syllables and carrying stress on the first of these two,” implying that all Mixtec varieties have the same stress behavior. (Carroll 2015:86. The unit named is the couplet, i.e. the disyllabic root; nothing carried from Josserand says whether the domain is the word or contrasts it with phrase promin…
5111.dloc: Carroll 2015 sec. 4.2.1, p. 86; sec. 4.2.2 p. 87 (Yoloxochitl final stress); Table A.2 p. 276. Penner 2019 pp. 91-92. Josserand 1983:180 itself not reached (ProQuest/UMI only).
5111.prule: No reachable source states a stress rule for Yutanduchi de Guerrero Mixtec. The only statement whose scope formally covers the variety is Josserand's (1983:180) definition of the Mixtec couplet as 'composed of two syllables and carrying stress on the first of these two', seen second-hand only: Carroll 2015:86 reads it as generalizing across the modern varieties of Josserand's survey (Yutanduchi = survey town Yutn, Table A.2 p. 276), Penner 2019:92 reads it as posited for Proto-Mixtec, and Carroll 2015:87 names Yoloxochitl as a Mixtec variety with final stress, so the generalization is not exceptionless. Carroll's variety-by-variety survey (p. 86: Nuxaa, Ayutla, Jicaltepec, Acatlan, Diuxi, Mixtepec, Atatlahuca, Silacayoapan, Alacatlatzala) does not include Yutanduchi, and McKendry 2001, the only reachable work with first-hand Yutanduchi data, says nothing about its stress. If the catalog ever admits the family-level statement as a proxy for the variety, the position is couplet-initial (first syllable of the disyllabic root; root-anchored, quantity-insensitive), which is set by morphology rather than fixed and quantity-insensitive, since it is defined on the couplet and not counted from a word edge.

5114.tone: Tone language with lexical tone classes and grammatical tone (number, TAM, polarity). Elnur & Compes 2026 posit three underlying level tones L, M, H; H is grammatical, barred word-initially, at the right edge of the root or on the final morpheme (FM); one surface exception (leftward-floating H in an alternative form of monosyllabic MH roots). Osman 2006 lists five surface tones (H, L, M, falling, rising), contours on short vowels, tone marking sg/pl. Neither source uses 'stress' or 'accent' of Beria: the only hits are the Yip (2002: 83) quotation 'accented or stressed syllables' (a general remark, p. 52), 'accent notation system of the Africanist tradition' (a notation remark, p. 36), and 'pitch-accent' said of Dazaga per Walters 2016 (p. 56), not of Beria. Orthographic only: the Beria Giray Erfe script proposal (Priest 2008, SIL L2/08-265, sec. E.2) lists 'U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE represents stress', and the SIL font page says 'Tone and stress marks are mutually exclusive. Tone markings occur in transcriptions, and stress markings occur in the writing system.' -- a writing-system mark with no placement rule.

tn.quote: Beria is a tone language and, for Wagi, three tone levels are attested: L, M, and H. On the surface, these three levels usually form tonal contours in two tone patterns (e.g., LM, LH, MH, ML), as well as some complex contours (e.g., LML and LHL). ... Beria as analyzed in this study exhibits a three-tone system in which the underlying level tones (L, M, and H) typically form tonal contour melodies on the surface. ... Since as a general rule the H tone is excluded from the word-initial position, Beria has no H-tone-only forms underlyingly.

5115.tone: Wannemacher 2010: four lexical tones (high-falling, high, mid, low), tense/modal phonation contrast; checked-syllable tone predictable from initial voicing and phonation; fn 11 (p. 90): in polysyllabic words tone is written only on the last syllable. Stress: only the negative statement that word-initial reduced CV syllables are unstressed. Wannemacher 1998 (Google Books, grade excerpt, not the record's basis): 'Zaiwa word-level stress is appropriate since stress is relevant in determining syllable structure. Stress is manifest as acoustic intensity, full vowel quality, and vowel length and does not necessarily correspond to pitch'; 'Zaiwa stressed syllables are the unmarked case. Unstressed syllables are the marked case, occurring with peripheral syllables'; 'Heavy and light syllables in Zaiwa correspond to stressed and unstressed syllables'; '(78) [+stress] = μμ [-stress] = μ'; §6.7 stress and tone = emotional emphasis raising pitch and loudness. I.e. every bimoraic (full) syllable is 'stressed' and only reduced Cə/V syllables are not: a weight-to-fullness correlation under a tone system, not a culminative stress-position rule. Lustig 2010 (excerpt): stressing a syllable = changing its tone to /55/ with weakening of a second syllable to /11/ (calling names, emphasis). JIPA 2025 (Ruili speaker; six tones 55/44/35/51/31/21) and Dai 2026 (Hounong) do not discuss stress.

5117.prule: No stress rule stated for Zangskari. 5118.dq: In ZZ, words are stressed on the penultimate syllable of their citation/prepausal form, which is the last syllable of their connected-speech/underlying form.

5118.prule: Fixed stress on the last syllable of the connected-speech/underlying word (the root syllable, since final vowels are deleted in connected speech); in citation/pre-pausal form, which adds an epenthetic final [a], this is uniformly the penultimate syllable. The author treats the connected-speech form as underlyingly basic (rule inversion: final [a] epenthesis).
5118.srule: Not mentioned in Operstein 2016 (IJAL 82(2)), secs. 2.1 and 4.3-4.4 read in full; the article's whole stress statement is the primary rule.
5118.quote: In present-day ZZ, the situation is more complex in that the final vowels are deleted in connected-speech forms and surface as [a] prepausally and in citation forms. Although the connected-speech form is historically the more recent of the two, it is taken to be underlyingly basic in the synchronic phonology of the language. ... 5123.tone: The author classifies Zbu as a tonal language of the word-tone ('African') type but stresses that it differs from most Sino-Tibetan tone languages 'par l’importance d’une position accentuée avec les corrélats usuels d’un accent dynamique (stress)'; footnote 1 (p. 74) follows Hyman (2009) in refusing the label 'pitch accent'. Acoustic correlates (pp. 76-77): F0 is the most distinct correlate; intensity/duration ('accent dynamique') is asymmetric — barely perceptible for final accent (oxytone/perispomenon), strongly marked for the paroxytone (final unaccented syllable much shorter and weaker, often breathy or devoiced); laryngeal state in pausa (glottal constriction for oxytones, lax/devoiced ending for perispomenon and paroxytone). Pre-accent syllables show a slight rise or stay flat. The two-way tone contrast (level vs falling) exists only on final-accented words.

5125.prule: Accent placement is set by morphological class and affix identity: an 'unaccented' word of two or more syllables takes the greater stress on the first syllable (General Rule 1), but verbs in conjugation and adjectives with verbal terminations take it on the last (conjugational) syllable; compounds of three or more syllables carry the lesser accent on the first and the greater on the middle syllable (Rule 2); the interrogative particle -mê 'almost invariably' takes the greater accent and the iterative infix -dai- takes the stress; disyllabic nouns move the accent from the first to the second syllable when case-endings are affixed (mi′nâ -> minâ′-kî), trisyllabic nouns do not (hâ′râg″di -> hâ′râg″di-kî) (Rule 5).
5125.srule: Soppitt marks two degrees of accent, the greater (″) and the lesser (′). In compound words of three or more syllables the lesser accent is on the first syllable and the greater on the middle (Hai′gâm″bau; likewise hâ′râg″di 'tiger', tâ′dai″gû 'will go again', tâ′gû mê″ 'will you go?'); with both -dai- and interrogative mê the lesser accent is on dai and the greater on mê (tâ-dai′-gû-mê″). Simple unaccented words carry a single (initial) stress; no rhythmic secondary stress is described.
5125.quote: General Rules. 1. When a word is unaccented, and contains more than one syllable, greater stress should be put on the first than on any of the others,—thus, “chûnâ,” “now.” Exceptions—(a)—Verbs in conjugation have, as a rule, the stress placed on the last syllable, e.g., “tâgû″,” “will go.” (b)—Adjectives when used with verbal terminations follow the above rule, and take the accent on the last syllable, thus “idâ″,” “is good.” 2. 5125.tone: Soppitt 1885 says nothing about tone; his 'greater' and 'lesser' accents are described as stress. Every modern primary description treats Zeme as a lexical tone language and has no stress or accent statement (a full-text search of the saved chapter texts: 'stress'/'accent' absent): Raguibou 2015 ch. 3 'There are three contrastive tones in Zeme. They are high /’/, mid...'; Chanu 2017 ch. 3 line 72 'Zeme has two tones i.e., raising and falling'; Muchahary 2019 ch. 3 'There are three tones in Zeme Naga i.e. rising, level and falling'. Soppitt's accent marks on suffixes and particles (the future suffix -gû, the question particle -mê) may well transcribe tone or intonation rather than stress.

tn.quote: Zeme is a tonal language with contrasting lexical elements. There are three tones in Zeme Naga i.e. rising, level and falling. The rising tone is marked as ( ́ ), the falling tone is marked as ( ̀ )and the level tone is unmarked. 3.7.1. Tone contrasts In order to prove the three tones in Zeme, the following contrasting tones have been established. … Rising /heká/ ‘fish’ … Level /heka/ ‘parrot’ … Falling /hekà/ ‘forest range’ … Rising tone in first syllable and falling tone in second syllable /zéirà/ ‘bed’
tn.cite: Muchahary, Francis. 2019. The phonology and morphology of Zeme Naga. PhD thesis, Assam University, Silchar (supervisor Paramita Purkait).
tn.locator: Ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.7 'Tone' and 3.7.1 'Tone contrasts', thesis pp. 65-68
tn.note: Three lexical tones, rising, level and falling, one per syllable, shown by minimal triplets; no statement on stress, downstep or tone sandhi. Other theses count 2 (rising/falling) or 3 (high/mid/low).
